title: Orient beach attack: South African swimmer killed by shark
description: A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.Janine Loc
body: A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London"."She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave."She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

schema.headline: Orient beach attack: South African swimmer killed by shark

title: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
description: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donal
body: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump."The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship. "Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote."If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her -  or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated."Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC. "The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe." Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation". But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago. Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

schema.headline: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'

title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, claims prosecutors
description: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support"
body: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the ChatGPT-maker, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and said a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.The 35-year-old engineer was deemed a flight risk and denied bail on Monday, pending a trial.The Saudi government did not respond to BBC requests for comment.Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official."Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued. US district judge Alex Tse on Monday denied Alfozan's attorneys request for his release on bail, saying "there is a risk of non-appearance that is significant".The FBI investigation is ongoing.Alfozan was scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine.

schema.headline: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, claims prosecutors

title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
description: US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" impo
body: US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada  broke down in August.The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".The White House has been contacted for comment.Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry."These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338. Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.It  also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency."No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada."The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

schema.headline: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge

title: Protesters and police in Albania fight in seventh day of violent clashes
description: Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes.The protesters, many of them high school and univ
body: Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes.The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence."The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen".A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation.The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack."In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait.A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters.Squads of riot police chased the predominantly student crowd through the park. Protesters took refuge in a cafe where even the eyes of the waiters streamed from the teargas.Under trees, volunteers in yellow reflector jackets stood their ground helping those overcome by the fumes. I watched a young man remonstrating with a policeman, who then fired pepper spray in his face at point-blank range."The police actions are often chaotic and stupid," human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani told the BBC. He provides legal support to more than 100 people who have been arrested."In court, the police rarely present evidence," he said. His clients include a man arrested on his way to a bus stop – completely unrelated to the protests, he said."Those who are actually throwing stuff at the police rarely get caught, because they run the fastest," Serjani said.Police appear as incensed by the violence against their colleagues as the protesters are by the strong-arm tactics of the police. The result is mayhem.Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her."In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK."The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said.She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it."When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said."They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up."At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down."We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups.Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said."I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said.Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it.

schema.headline: Protesters and police in Albania fight in seventh day of violent clashes

title: Jane Doe says embattled Cornell head Kotlikoff doubted her gang-rape claim
description: In a two-page letter dated 14 October and obtained by the BBC, Doe told the faculty senate that after she reported the alleged rape, she received "a s
body: In a two-page letter dated 14 October and obtained by the BBC, Doe told the faculty senate that after she reported the alleged rape, she received "a second-hand account" of Kotlikoff's reaction and that his "initial response" was "along the lines of, 'Why did she wait so long to report it?'"Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police on 8 November, about three weeks after the fraternity party.She noted that Kotlikoff had a conversation with the then-president of her sorority and that other staff members were present, at least one of whom "appeared distressed" by the college president's question.Doe said in her letter: "It diminished my confidence in the administration's ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school."She said she wrote the letter so that faculty "can make an informed choice" ahead of their 28 October vote on whether to express no confidence in Kotlikoff's leadership.The university confirmed receipt of the letter from Doe's lawyer.But in a statement to the BBC, a Cornell spokesperson said: "The second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account." The spokesperson said Kotlikoff's question about the delay in reporting the alleged rape "was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell's anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024"."He was not questioning Jane Doe's reporting," the spokesperson said.Kotlikoff, who has led the Ithaca-based institution for 26 years, was grilled by the faculty senate last Wednesday.Staff said they were "deeply disturbed" by his handling of the case and accused him of lacking an "emotional response", according to recordings obtained by the BBC.Kotlikoff highlighted changes the university had introduced as a result of Doe's allegations, including banning fraternity parties. "We are all extraordinarily upset by the events at Cornell in October of 2024," he said. The faculty senate, a governing body composed of professors and other academic staff at Cornell, scheduled their no-confidence vote for 28 October.In recordings of the meeting, faculty said sexual misconduct on campus was a systemic problem that demanded "systemic attention".Paul Ortiz, a labour history professor who sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said students had told faculty they "feel unsafe walking to the library after dark".He accused Cornell of treating rape "as more of a 'PR problem' than a heinous crime".

schema.headline: Jane Doe says embattled Cornell head Kotlikoff doubted her gang-rape claim

title: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
description: Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.  "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk sa
body: Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.  "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday.While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move."The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.    That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia.US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions.Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google.The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year.

schema.headline: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX

title: Alberta's decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump
description: "Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red an
body: "Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red and white "Forever Canadian" banners.It's a message that appears to have struck a chord with the electorate, as preliminary results show more than two-thirds of Alberta voters said they want to remain a part of Canada.But the future of the federation does still rest on its richest province.Alberta, with most of Canada's proven oil reserves and abundant gas and mineral wealth, is playing a pivotal role in Ottawa's drive to survive a punishing trade war with the US by diversifying trade, strengthening its economy, and forging new alliances on the other side of the world.Carney, the former central banker who grew up in Alberta, is now Canada's builder-in-chief – at home, and beyond its borders.Note the emphasis in his first statement after Monday's vote on separation in the province, as soon as the scale of the victory was clear: "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other."Albertans' overwhelming "yes" to stay in Canada gives him political bricks and mortar, too."Don't mess with Canada," warned Thomas Lukaszuk, a former lawmaker whose Forever Canadian campaign played a key role in this referendum's outcome.Addressing elated supporters in Edmonton, the provincial capital, as the "yes" count for Canada kept tumbling in, Lukaszuk underlined that this vote "will send a very strong message to the rest of the world".Everyone knows he's talking about the troublesome neighbour to the south – in particular its president, who keeps threatening to turn Canada into the 51st US state.The same day Albertans were voting on their future in Canada, Trump sent his own signal north at a rally in Kansas ahead of next month's US midterm polls."I will let you keep ice hockey, and I will let you keep your 'O Canada' national anthem," he promised before adding: "We're only kidding."For Canadians, it's no laughing matter.In the run up to this referendum, Carney reiterated a warning he's often sounded that "there are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they own us" – even if he didn't spell out who "they" is.He didn't have to.And, in this defining time for the separatist camp, some in their ranks didn't hide their direction of travel. Some of their most prominent leaders admitted they travelled to Washington three times last year to meet US State Department officials and outline what an independent Alberta could offer – including a possible oil pipeline through the US to the Pacific.But the rest of the world may take only passing notice of what was, for Canada, an historic vote sparking conversations and concerns across the country, from coast to coast to coast."Short of a vote to separate, most foreign governments, with the exception of the United States, have little interest in domestic Canadian politics," says Professor Janice Stein, founding director of the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto."Foreign investors are focused on the time it will take to complete major infrastructure projects, a return on investment, and predictable regulations," she explains in a nod to Carney's long list of megaprojects he hopes will eventually turbocharge economic growth. They're all costly; many will take years to build.An ambitious blueprint already includes a proposed pipeline to the Pacific coast which opens opportunities for Alberta's oil to reach Asian markets – a move which also addresses Alberta's long-standing grievance that its economy has been stifled by federal policies, including environmental regulations.At a rally in Alberta last week, it was Carney's comment that the pipeline "will reduce our dependence on the United States" that triggered the loudest and longest applause of the night.After Monday's vote, Carney – the former UN Special Envoy for Climate Action and Finance –   pointed to "unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta as its core". Political and economic pressures now seem to eclipse his green credentials."Build Canada Strong" has been Carney's mantra ever since he first entered politics, a complete neophyte, at the start of last year.At home there are possible wide-reaching repercussions from the final tallies in the referendum's nine other questions which dealt with issues ranging from greater provincial powers, the costs of immigration, and potential constitutional changes.Those results are certain to provoke debate, and deal making or breaking, involving Canada's nine other provinces and three territories. They all have their own grievances, too.The prime minister has had to defend himself when journalists ask if he is spending too much time on foreign trips with his charm offensive to build new political alliances and trade partnerships, including an unprecedented and still uncertain offer of associate membership of the European Union."I can do both and I need to do both," he recently replied with his signature bluntness before listing the more than 16 bills which went through Parliament in the last session dealing with everything from major tax changes, public safety, and the price of fuel.For now, Carney is riding high in the polls at home – including in Alberta, which doesn't traditionally support his Liberal party - in a long "political honeymoon" other beleaguered politicians would envy.And the plain-speaking politician's strong and steady response to Trump threats, including retaliatory tariffs, has seen his star rising on the world stage. It's an unexpected turn for a country which has often been missing from top tables and has sometimes even been dismissed as "boring".The Economist magazine decided to put Carney on their cover, on this week of weeks for Canada, with a perfect red maple leaf between his teeth."Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world," reads one of its headlines, with an article which also focuses on Canada's "vulnerabilities" including Alberta's ballot."The broader takeaway from this vote might be that Canadian unity is in fine shape," remarks David Moscrop, political scientist and author of the forthcoming book On Nationalism."But what happens after Donald Trump is gone and Canada no longer has a single, bombastic target which drives Canadians to rally around the flag?" he asks.Carney's decision to recently walk away from trade talks with the US gave rise to another swell of Canadian pride and patriotism. But if this trade war drags on with a country which traditionally takes 70% of Canada's exports, Canadians will feel even greater pain in their daily lives.But today is a day to vigorously wave the maple leaf flag."It's a win for Team Canada and its resilience," commented CBC journalist Janyce McGregor during the public broadcaster's rolling coverage.

schema.headline: Alberta's decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump

title: Zelensky says intelligence sharing 'works now' as US envoy to meet Putin in Russia
description: Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks in Oslo alongside the Norwegian prime minister, said "genuine progress" had been ma
body: Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks in Oslo alongside the Norwegian prime minister, said "genuine progress" had been made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details, and warned that patience would be needed.Witkoff was not present at their joint press conference with Zelensky after the talks, nor was President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner who had attended via video link. A US official later said the meeting had been "very productive and constructive" and that there was a "strong alignment at the working level" between the US, Ukraine and Europe on "next steps". Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that President Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.Speaking after the news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal".He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.Russian drone attacks have continued this week. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed on Tuesday - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.Another attack overnight on Wednesday killed two more people near Kharkiv, the country's second-largest city.Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now"."Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," he said.Zelensky also said he hoped for a good result on Starlink, after Ukraine's military had reported speed restrictions on drones using its internet network to conduct strikes against Russia.A bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into the restrictions last week.The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine had also been discussed, as well as energy ceasefire proposals, and restated that Kyiv was "ready for negotiations" to end the conflict. "Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said.Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre meanwhile stressed that Europe needed "to be at the table" during any discussions about how to bring the fighting to an end.Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine, but stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.European leaders have meanwhile expressed concern about recent US statements towards Russia.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war on Monday, and said that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly"."It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy"."We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said.

schema.headline: Zelensky says intelligence sharing 'works now' as US envoy to meet Putin in Russia

title: Helen Haines: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says
description: Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirme
body: Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.Phil Haines said the"horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated. "She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund."Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance. He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord.Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established."His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush."Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court."Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said.Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines.Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional seat of Indi in Victoria. They described the apparent attack as "devastating and unfathomable".The incident occurred on Monday afternoon at around 15.35, local time. Moments after the car hit Haines, bystanders pulled Nugent out of the vehicle and detained him.Jacob and Jackie Evans were among the first on the scene, and said Haines was grateful to them for coming to her aid as she lay severely injured. "Thank you, you lovely people," is what Haines said to them, according to the Herald Sun."She was thanking us, it was incredible," Jackie told Nine's Today programme.Jacob used a tourniquet he had in a medical kit in his car to help stem the bleeding from one of Haines's legs.Haines underwent surgery after the incident and lost one of her legs. As of Wednesday morning she has also lost the other leg, her husband Phil told reporters.The community in Wangaratta, as well as the wider political community, are in shock over the incident in a country where political violence is rare.Leaders from across the political spectrum have paid tribute to Haines, who was first elected in 2019 and is well regarded by her peers.Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had spoken to Haines's husband several times since the incident.In an interview with the national broadcaster ABC, Albanese said threats to female politicians were marked by a "different form of vilification and aggression" such as threats of rape.There has also been a recent growing trend of threats against "high office holders", with almost one person a week being charged for such offences, police said.Monday's incident has sparked debate over the level of security for MPs.Federal police said that individual protection for every one of the country's 226 federal MPs would require "incredible" levels of staffing.Instead, police assess the need for close personal protection based on a person's role and the threat environment around them, police said.Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the same press conference as Haines' husband, said this was "a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better". "We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened," she says."Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency."

schema.headline: Helen Haines: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says

title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capitalByPaul AdamsDiplomatic correspondentThe hug that Trump envoy Steve Wi
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capitalByPaul AdamsDiplomatic correspondentThe hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?Both in rhetoric and actions, the past ten days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.Just listen to the way they talk about each other."Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.The verbal assault has continued this week."Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister"."Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever."We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?In some ways, we've been here before.After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.Figure caption, Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says TrumpLast Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin."What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC."It's inexplicable and saddening."Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking."We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink.A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.Image source, EPAImage caption, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued unabatedA decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things.""There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink."I think we will have good results too," he said.Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

schema.headline: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism

title: France is divided over who to blame for weekend riots
description: "This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us
body: "This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October. I'd stopped Elisabeth and her friend to ask their thoughts on what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears."My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.The president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend. French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black, folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left. It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections. LFI denies this.The mass looting of what is said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity?Emmanuel Macron, who is on his way out as president and viewed by many in France as a lame duck, and his government are accused of dropping the ball and failing to keep the country safe on Saturday.Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice.Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts have led former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence. Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's interior minister, Bernard Quintin, warned of the "TikTokisation" of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liège on "known far-left groups".In France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire", said Nuñez. On Tuesday Lecornu spoke of  "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups". Previously he had accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos. It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied.Mélenchon took part in Saturday's planned protest. Politicians from his LFI movement have been present at the student demonstrations since they started a month ago in the socially deprived outskirts of Paris, with demands for better state education for all.In Saint-Denis suburb on Monday, I met Lisa Cordat, of the FSE student union. She told me that students had organised themselves for demos via social media messaging or through student-led organisations. She said it was "insulting" to suggest they were being manipulated or "told to do this, or do that" by politicians. "Student anger comes from the ground up," says Lisa.But there is also a palpable frustration amongst many in France at what they see as the politicisation of Saturday's violence. Lina, who is 25, told me: "Politicians are hunting for scapegoats but don't ask why it all happened. The root causes of Saturday. We feel scared and abandoned."France's leading politicians have indulged in a festival of finger-pointing since Saturday.The presidential election here in six months' time is hotly contested and the volatility on French streets funneled immediately into France's already febrile politics.Mélenchon, currently running in second place in most polls, ahead of centrist candidates, accused France's centrist prime minister of being "responsible for the chaos" either due to "incompetence or a worst-case strategy." Mélenchon went on to apparently imply Lecornu may have allowed the violence to unfold, so as to position itself as a "party of order", after Saturday's lawlessness, "that would make people forget his failure in public finances".France is struggling with spiralling public debt and government borrowing costs.As for intelligence failures on Saturday, President Macron has demanded explanations and a new policing strategy. France's interior minister admitted there were not enough officers on the streets, despite the nationwide protests being publicised well in advance. Following accusations of heavy-handedness at earlier demos, the police seemed very much out of their depth this weekend.Of all the presidential hopefuls, it would seem Marine Le Pen of the anti-immigration National Rally party gains most politically from Saturday's shocking scenes.She is already way ahead in opinion polls. Le Pen chose to launch a presidential-looking video address to the nation via social media on Sunday. Dressed formally, behind a large desk and in front of a French flag, she blamed Jean-Luc Mélenchon by name for his associates who "look to throw the country into chaos," she said. She also accused the Macron government of "running out of steam", meaning that France was "taken hostage between violence and powerlessness". She ended her video by reminding French voters they would have the opportunity to "choose a different path" in six months' time.Le Pen's party promotes a law and order, closed-border message and, like US President Donald Trump and US Vice President JD Vance, has blamed migrants, amongst others, for the chaos in France on Saturday. French authorities have not implicated migrants in the violence.One teacher called Mar complained that Saturday's violence "suits politicians' purpose. It distracts from weeks of legitimate protests for better public services", she said. "Politicians aren't listening to what the students need, or what teachers need or what the French people want. They're using the violence to election-campaign to become president and to try to make their opponents look bad."But increasing numbers in France, many amongst the young Gen Z generation, say they have dwindling faith in "the system". That's something we see echoed in other European countries where mainly youth-led protests erupted - some violently - this weekend in Italy, Portugal and Albania as well as France and Belgium. These demonstrations are often triggered by spiralling living costs, deteriorating public services and a sense of powerlessness people feel over their own lives. What can we do as individuals about our rising energy costs caused by wars far away in the Middle East or in Ukraine, many ask. Voters increasingly say they are losing faith in traditional or governing political parties to listen to concerns and address them. The young look at climate change, social inequality, impossible housing prices and AI potentially threatening their place in the job market.According to opinion polls conducted by this year by Pew, 69% of people in France are dissatisfied with democracy. In Spain, it's 68% and in Italy, 62%. The US is experiencing similar disillusionment with 69% saying they are dissatisfied with how democracy is working.So many people I've spoken to in France since Saturday's riots emphasise the importance in making a clear distinction between angry but peaceful protesters, and those intent on wreaking violent havoc.Politics aside, is what we're now seeing in Europe's protest wave perhaps a powerful cocktail of a bubbling over of frustration, cries for help for the authorities to listen but also, for some, a dark sense there's little left to lose?

schema.headline: France is divided over who to blame for weekend riots

title: Borneo burning: Life on the frontline of South East Asia's toxic haze
description: Image caption, Firefighters have been battling the stubborn blaze for weeks now ByLiza TambunanIndonesia correspondent Reporting fromCentral Kalimanta
body: Image caption, Firefighters have been battling the stubborn blaze for weeks now ByLiza TambunanIndonesia correspondent Reporting fromCentral Kalimantan  and Gavin Butler When the sun hits the smog enveloping Indonesian Borneo, it turns everything the colour of rust. Cars, houses and streets appear and disappear out of a dim russet fog. There are few better words than "apocalyptic" to describe the way this looks.But it's at night, in the quiet darkness, that mother-of-three Dianyra Eka Nastiti grows most fearful."Sometimes at night my baby's chest makes a rattling sound," she says. "She was hospitalised for bronchopneumonia when she was just a month and a half old, and every single night I worry: Will my child cough tomorrow?"Those thoughts haunt me every night."Nastiti lives in Palangkaraya, at the frontline of a months-long environmental catastrophe that has blanketed large parts of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze.Wildfires have torched some 1.9 million hectares across Indonesia since the start of the year, according to open-access satellite platform Nusantara Atlas – an area roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey, or the entire landmass of Fiji. One million hectares are thought to have burned in September alone.But the toxic fallout is larger still. Swathes of smouldering forest, swamp and peatlands have turned the air thick with microparticles and carbon monoxide, creating a noxious cloud that has swaddled Indonesia and drifted as far as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.As of mid-October, Indonesia's Health Ministry had recorded more than 277,000 cases of people suffering from chronic coughs and acute respiratory infections. More than 62,000 of those were infants and toddlers under the age of five."The forest fires have had a huge impact, especially on everyone's health," says 22-year-old Natari Victoria, who was admitted to a health centre in Palangkarya after suffering from a cough for more than a week."I have young cousins, including babies, who are coughing too. It's really taking a toll on them."Image caption, Dianyra Eka Nastiti is worried about how her children will recover Haze and smoke from peat fires contain a complex mixture of pollutants that pose serious health risks to the human body. Among these are tiny microparticles which can penetrate deep into the lungs and, in some cases, enter the bloodstream, causing inflammation, chronic lung diseases and increased risk of premature death.Another concern is the toxic greenhouse gases that are being unleashed into the air."Here in Central Kalimantan, especially in Palangkaraya, the sky has turned yellow and hazy," says Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office. "So what are the residents actually breathing in? It's not fresh oxygen; it's carbon dioxide and pollutants. And what happens as a result? The body – specifically the brain – doesn't get enough oxygen."Children, older adults and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the dangers of haze, especially during prolonged periods of exposure, when the health impacts can accumulate.In places like Palangkarya, the official advice is to stay indoors and avoid going out. But Nastiti says this is unrealistic."I still need to buy vegetables, stock up on food, purchase school supplies, and take care of other necessities," she explains. "It's simply not possible, and I feel like the people who say things like that have no idea what is actually happening here."Nastiti's utmost priority, however, is the health and wellbeing of her children. And when the haze grows heavy, she is quick to force them inside."With conditions being so unsafe, I have no choice," she says. "Our young children should be at the park, playing with their friends and going to school. Instead, they are locked inside the house."Lola Macitri, a 37-year-old who lives in the rural village of Ramang, 50km (31 miles) north of Palangkaraya, has been similarly housebound. As the smog has deepened over the past few weeks – from dusty grey to amber yellow and, more recently, burnt orange – she and her family have come to spend most of their time indoors.Her children, like many others in Indonesia's more haze-affected areas, have been doing their school classes online, she says, while she and other adults struggle to manage half-a-day's work out in the poisonous air.Image caption, People have been turning up at hospitals after complaining of feeling sick from the toxic smog    Countless farmers, daily-wage earners and small vendors have similarly been forced to either sacrifice their livelihoods or endure the risk of stepping outside. Beyond that, many are left with no choice but to wait out the storm."If you ask whether we are afraid of the health risks, of course we are. But where else can we go?" says Macitri. "We just have to endure and stay strong through this situation, because there is simply no other option."The government is under mounting pressure from the public to do more to stop the fires, with many criticising what they see as a woefully inadequate response by the authorities.Authorities insist they have pursued a range of measures to try to extinguish the flames and, in turn, the smoke – from aerial waterbombing to experimental weather modification. Last week, the Indonesian government said it had deployed more than 60,000 personnel to carry out a "land operation", claiming they'd achieved an 80% success rate in extinguishing new fires."At this point, I think we need to use every safe and effective option available to suppress the fires," says Dr Nisa Novita, a forestry expert and peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN)."It's a bit like trying to save a sinking ship: we need to act urgently, use whatever tools can help, and prevent further damage while we still can."But those resources are fast depleting for responders on the ground.For more than 100 days, Juni has been fighting wildfires that show only false signs of abating. On the surface, the flames are out – but underground, smouldering blazes continue to burn through a deep understory of carbon, vegetation and peat."It is truly exhausting," he says, describing how the relentless smoke has produced in him a shortness of breath, a persistent cough and an unshakeable pain in his eyes. When asked what he needs, he says "air"."The haze makes it hard to breathe," he explains. "We are just hoping for heavy rain."Image caption, Wildfires have been devastating Indonesia's Central Kalimantan regionThousands of others across Indonesia and Southeast Asia have spent the past several months hoping for the same.Seasonal wildfires are not new to Indonesia but this year, a so-called Super El Nino has amplified drought conditions and delayed the kind of rainfall that is critical to extinguishing peat fires. It has also made things exponentially harder for those at the coalface, like Juni, who have spent months battling a seemingly irrepressible fire front.Dr Novita explains that conditions on the ground have become much harsher even in recent weeks, as the prolonged drought makes water increasingly scarce.Fauzi Rahman, another firefighter in Palangkaraya, highlighted this as one of the main difficulties confronting him and his peers."Peatland fires are hard to put out because they require a lot of water and a long time," he says. "On regular land we can clear 20 hectares in a single day, especially with a large team... On peatland, it can take months."We really have to inject water deep down, all the way to the bottom, which requires a huge amount of water. And right now, water is hard to find."What's more concerning for Dr Novita, however, is that her team has reported fires spreading into areas where there has been no history of fire before."So we're not only dealing with fires in the usual hotspots but also seeing them emerge in new areas," she says.In Palangkaraya, people are growing desperate for an end to this apocalypse. But it will likely take a force of nature for that to happen any time soon.Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office, tells the BBC that "hopefully, with all the extraordinary efforts from the community, the military, and the police working together, the fires can be put out"."However, as of right now, the fires are still burning," he adds. "So what can we hope for? Our greatest hope is that Almighty God will bring us rain soon."Image caption, Firefighters have been battling the stubborn blaze for weeks now

schema.headline: Borneo burning: Life on the frontline of South East Asia's toxic haze

title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
description: Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.The second hand re-selling pla
body: Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend."The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage. Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses. Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast. "Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC."When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."France is one of Vinted's largest markets, along with the UK and Italy.The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen.

schema.headline: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale

title: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda
description: A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.Robert K
body: A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend. The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety."It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics."Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

schema.headline: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda
